name: Grading Calibration
title: Grading Calibration
answer: Grading calibration is the practice of teachers who teach the same course scoring student work consistently, so a student's grade does not depend on which teacher they have. It matters because it builds fairness across a department and gives teachers a shared way to check whether an AI scoring tool agrees with their own judgment. Calibration sessions use discussion among teachers, not a special product, to reach that consistency.

sections.body: Grading calibration addresses the problem that teachers of the same course may score similar work differently. In calibration sessions, teachers score the same samples of student work and then discuss where their scores and reasoning differ. The aim is consistency, so a student's grade is not tied to the teacher they happen to be assigned. AI can help by organizing samples or summarizing points of disagreement, but it does not replace the session. The value comes from teachers hearing each other's reasoning and adjusting their own practice.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not give grade bands, so the practice is described for teachers who share a course. A department gathers samples of student work and has each teacher score them independently. The teachers then meet to compare scores and talk through the differences. AI may be used to arrange the samples or to produce a summary of where teachers disagreed. The same samples can also be used to test an AI scoring feature, by comparing its scores with the teachers' calibrated scores.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, study, figure, or finding for grading calibration. It presents the idea as practice rather than research. The support offered is practical: no special product is needed, and any department can run the comparison between an AI scoring tool and calibrated teacher scores. So the case rests on professional practice, not on a cited research base.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: AI is a support for calibration, not a replacement for it. The discussion among teachers is where calibration actually happens, so a department should not let a tool take over that conversation. If an AI scoring feature disagrees with teachers who have calibrated their scores, the text says the tool needs adjustment or should not be used. The decisions about scoring, adjustment, and whether to use a tool stay with the teachers and the department. No special product is required, and the practical test is available to any department.
